Port-Royal
por-roy-AL
proper noun (a Jansenist centre)
From the convent of Port-Royal near Paris, the spiritual centre of French Jansenism in the seventeenth century, associated with Blaise Pascal.

📖 Biblical Definition

Port-Royal was a convent near Paris that became, in the seventeenth century, the spiritual and intellectual centre of French Jansenism, the Augustinian reform movement within the Roman Catholic Church associated with Blaise Pascal and the theologians of the “Port-Royal logic.” The Jansenists, drawing on Augustine's doctrines of sin and grace, recovered against the prevailing Jesuit theology much that the Reformed also hold: the depth of human depravity, the bondage of the will, the necessity and efficacy of sovereign grace, and predestination. The dictionary treats Port-Royal with a careful, sympathetic discrimination. There is much in the Jansenist movement the dictionary commends, for it stood for the very truths of grace that Rome had largely abandoned: that no man can come to Christ except the Father draw him, that salvation is not by works of righteousness but according to His mercy, and that He which begins a good work will perform it. These are the doctrines of grace, and the dictionary rejoices wherever they are found. Yet Port-Royal remained within the Roman communion, never breaking from the papacy, the Mass, or the sacramental system, and so its recovery of Augustinian grace was hindered and incomplete, condemned at last by Rome itself. The dictionary marks Port-Royal as a sobering and hopeful witness: hopeful, that the truth of sovereign grace cannot be wholly extinguished and broke out even within Rome; sobering, that to recover the doctrines of grace while remaining bound to a system that denies justification by faith alone is to build on a divided foundation. The Lord knoweth them that are His, and there were doubtless His own at Port-Royal; yet the dictionary holds that the doctrines of grace are rightly housed only in a church reformed by the whole Word of God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The convent near Paris that was the centre of French Jansenism, the Augustinian movement (associated with Pascal) that recovered the doctrines of grace within Rome; commended for those truths, yet hindered by remaining bound to the Roman system.

PORT-ROYAL, proper noun. A convent near Paris, the centre of French Jansenism in the seventeenth century.

Associated with Blaise Pascal and the “Port-Royal logic.”

The Jansenists recovered Augustinian doctrines of sin, grace, and predestination.

Commended for the doctrines of grace (John 6:44; Titus 3:5) Rome had abandoned.

Yet it remained within the Roman communion and was condemned by Rome.

📖 Key Scripture

Joh 6:44 — "No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day."

Tit 3:5 — "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;"

Php 1:6 — "Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:"

2 Ti 2:19 — "Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Port-Royal recovered the doctrines of grace yet remained bound to the Roman system—the papacy, the Mass, the sacramental scheme—so that its Augustinian revival was hindered, incomplete, and condemned by Rome.

expand to see more

The dictionary commends much in Port-Royal and the Jansenist movement it housed. Against the man-exalting theology of the Jesuits, the Jansenists recovered from Augustine the very truths the Reformed confess: the depth of human depravity, the bondage of the will, the sovereignty and efficacy of grace, and predestination. That no man comes to Christ but as the Father draws him, that God saves not by works but according to His mercy, that He who begins the good work will finish it—these are the doctrines of grace, and the dictionary rejoices that they broke out even within Rome, a proof that the truth of sovereign grace cannot be wholly extinguished.

Yet the dictionary marks the limitation that made the Jansenist recovery hindered and finally tragic. Port-Royal never broke from the Roman communion: it kept the papacy, the Mass, the sacramental system, and the Tridentine framework that denies justification by faith alone. To recover the doctrines of grace while remaining bound to a church that anathematized the gospel of grace is to build on a divided foundation, and Rome itself eventually condemned and dispersed them. The Lord knoweth them that are His, and there were surely His own at Port-Royal; but the dictionary holds that the doctrines of grace are rightly and safely housed only in a church reformed by the whole counsel of God, not in one that confesses sovereign grace with one breath and denies justification by faith with the next.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the convent of Port-Royal (Port-Royal-des-Champs and Port-Royal de Paris), the centre of Jansenism; named for the doctrines of Cornelius Jansen, revived from Augustine.

expand to see more

Port-Royal, the convent near Paris, centre of French Jansenism.

Jansenism, the Augustinian movement named for Cornelius Jansen.

Blaise Pascal, its most famous defender, author of the Provincial Letters.

Recovered the doctrines of grace against Jesuit theology.

Remained within Rome and was at last condemned and suppressed.

Usage

"The teacher commended Port-Royal's recovery of the doctrines of grace within Rome."

"He noted that the Jansenists confessed sovereign grace yet kept the Roman system that denies it."

"She saw in Port-Royal a proof that the truth of grace cannot be wholly extinguished."
